The Thorn-tailed rayadito (Aphrastura spinicauda) is a small insectivorous ovenbird endemic to the temperate forests of southern South America. Under the stable thermal conditions of the nest cavity, eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] require approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days] to hatch, a developmental period that aligns with the altricial mode of this species. Newly hatched nestlings emerge with a wet weight at birth of 2.1 grams [Wwb = 2.1 grams], reflecting the relatively undeveloped state typical of passerine hatchlings that depend entirely on parental brooding and feeding. This modest initial mass stands in contrast to the ultimate wet weight of 11 grams [Wwi = 11 grams] attained by fully grown adults, representing a greater than fivefold increase in body mass over the course of the nestling and fledgling periods. The rapid mass gain is supported by the high provisioning rates of both parents, who deliver arthropod prey throughout the daylight hours.

Field studies conducted over two breeding seasons in Navarino Island have provided detailed information on the reproductive timing and output of this species. At the species' typical active body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], fledging occurs at 21.8 days after hatching [tx = 21.8 days after hatching], though the literature reports a broader range of 16 to 23 days depending on local food availability and brood size. Sexual maturation, marking the onset of gonadal development, is achieved at 65.4 days after hatching [tp = 65.4 days after hatching] under the same thermal regime at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively rapid progression from hatching to nutritional independence is characteristic of many cavity-nesting furnariids that face intense competition for limited nest sites.

The reproductive strategy of the Thorn-tailed rayadito is characterized by a moderate investment per breeding attempt coupled with the potential for multiple broods within a single season. Females typically lay between 3 and 6 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 3 and 6 eggs per clutch], and under favorable environmental conditions, they may produce 2 clutches per year [F_R_i = 2 clutches per year]. This dual-clutching strategy allows the species to exploit extended periods of high arthropod abundance in the austral summer, thereby maximizing annual reproductive output. The time since birth at first brood, recorded at 365 days [tR = 365 days] when individuals are maintained at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], indicates that most birds defer their first breeding attempt until their second calendar year, a pattern common among small-to-medium-sized passerines that prioritize somatic development and territory acquisition during their first summer.

Comparative life-history analyses place the Thorn-tailed rayadito within a broader ecological context relative to other members of the Furnariidae. The maximum lifespan in the wild, based on recapture data from long-term banding studies, reaches 3,650 days [am = 3,650 days] at an active body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], which corresponds to approximately ten years of sustained reproductive activity. This longevity is notable given the species' small body size of 11 grams [Wwi = 11 grams], as most passerines of similar mass have lifespans of only three to five years in natural populations. The extended lifespan likely reflects the benefits of cavity nesting, which reduces predation risk on both adults and broods, and the relatively stable, low-disturbance environment of the sub-Antarctic forests. One consequence of this extended reproductive window is the opportunity for repeated breeding attempts across multiple seasons, allowing individuals to accumulate substantial lifetime reproductive success.

Ecological factors such as territory quality and local climate exert considerable influence on the demographic parameters reported for this species. Populations breeding in secondary-growth forests with high understory density tend to show earlier ages at first reproduction, occasionally producing their first brood at approximately 365 days since birth [tR = approximately 365 days since birth] when the active body temperature is around 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. In contrast, individuals from more marginal habitats delay breeding until their third year, presumably due to the greater energetic demands of territory acquisition. The combination of clutch size and clutch frequency yields an annual reproductive output of up to 12 eggs per year, though in practice most pairs achieve substantially lower rates owing to nest failure, brood reduction, and the energetic costs of multiple brooding. Future research linking thermal physiology to reproductive phenology will clarify how this species responds to ongoing climatic shifts in its Andean range.
